expectedText:
LIVING TRUST FUNDING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan T. Reyes · The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust

DECLARATION — INFORMATION SHEET ON FUNDING A TRUST
This information sheet describes the legal mechanics of transferring (“funding”) property into The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust, a trust Jordan T. Reyes created as settlor, naming Jordan T. Reyes as trustee, executed on January 15, 2026. Funding a trust — the act of moving specific property into the trustee's name — is a separate legal step from creating the trust itself, which is addressed in this corpus's own Revocable Living Trust document rather than here. The property this information sheet concerns is described as follows: Real property at 123 Main Street, Sacramento, California. This information sheet does not itself transfer any property into The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust, does not determine whether any specific item of property is or is not currently held in The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust, and preparing or signing it has no legal effect on the ownership of any asset.

HOW A TRUST IS CREATED, AND WHY CREATION ALONE DOESN'T FUND IT
California law recognizes several distinct methods of creating a trust, including a declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds that property as trustee, and a lifetime transfer of property by the owner to another person as trustee. Both methods share a common feature relevant to funding: each one operates only on property the settlor actually owned and either declared held in trust or actually transferred to the trustee. A trust instrument that identifies The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust, names Jordan T. Reyes as trustee, and even attaches a schedule listing specific property does not, by any of these statutory methods, itself bring listed property into the trust unless that property was actually, and correctly, transferred or declared held in trust — property merely referenced in The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust's schedule, without a completed transfer, has not become trust property under any of these methods.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Subject to other provisions of this chapter, a trust may be created by any of the following methods: (a) A declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds the property as trustee. (b) A transfer of property by the owner during the owner’s lifetime to another person as trustee. (c) A transfer of property by the owner, by will or by other instrument taking effect upon the death of the owner, to another person as trustee. (d) An exercise of a power of appointment to another person as trustee. (e) An enforceable promise to create a trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15200 (California Legislative Information text), the statutory methods of creating a trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15200.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California actually structures trust creation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust or its funding. This is a single statutory section (§ 15200); no additional independent source was found for this. A related, separate mechanism exists for property that was never funded during the settlor's lifetime but that the settlor's will directs into the trust at death (a “pour-over” provision, addressed in this corpus's own Revocable Living Trust document, not repeated here) — that mechanism routes probate property into the trust after death; it does not avoid probate for that property, and it is a different legal path from the lifetime-funding mechanics this document describes. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself transfer any property into any trust, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property.

REAL PROPERTY: A WRITTEN, SIGNED INSTRUMENT IS REQUIRED TO TRANSFER TITLE
Under California property law, an estate in real property — other than a short-term tenancy at will or for a year or less — can be transferred only by operation of law or by a written instrument, signed by the person disposing of it (or by that person's agent, if the agent's authority is itself in writing). Naming The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust as a beneficiary in a will, describing real property in The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust's schedule of assets, or simply intending for real property to belong to The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust does not, by itself, satisfy this requirement. A separate deed, in writing and signed by Jordan T. Reyes, conveying the specific real property from Jordan T. Reyes individually to Jordan T. Reyes as trustee of The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust, is what this statute requires to move title to real property into the trustee's name.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An estate in real property, other than an estate at will or for a term not exceeding one year, can be transferred only by operation of law, or by an instrument in writing, subscribed by the party disposing of the same, or by his agent thereunto authorized by writing."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1091 (California Legislative Information text), the written-instrument requirement to transfer an estate in real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1091.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own written-instrument requirement for transferring real property — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property or a specific trust. This is a single statutory section (§ 1091); no additional independent source was found for this, though a related statute on the separate, additional formality requirement for a trust of real property specifically (Cal. Prob. Code § 15206) appears elsewhere in this corpus's Revocable Living Trust document and is not repeated here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself transfer any property into any trust, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property.

WHAT RECORDING A DEED DOES — AND DOESN'T DO — TO A TRANSFER
An executed but unrecorded deed conveying real property from Jordan T. Reyes to Jordan T. Reyes as trustee of The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust is not, for that reason alone, ineffective as between Jordan T. Reyes and Jordan T. Reyes: California law treats an unrecorded instrument as valid between the parties to it and anyone else who has notice of it. Recording instead does two other things: it protects the transfer against being cut off by a later purchaser or mortgagee who pays value in good faith and records first, and it is what makes the county's public record — the record that title companies, lenders, and the property tax assessor rely on — show Jordan T. Reyes, rather than Jordan T. Reyes individually, as the owner of record.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An unrecorded instrument is valid as between the parties thereto and those who have notice thereof."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1217 (California Legislative Information text), an unrecorded instrument remains valid between the parties and anyone with notice of it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1217.)
  "Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1214 (California Legislative Information text), an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good-faith purchaser or mortgagee who records first (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1214.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of what recording actually does under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel or transfer. § 1217 and § 1214 are two different statutory sections (both within the same Civil Code chapter on the effect of recording), not subsections of one section, so they are presented here as two separate, corroborating sources rather than one. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself execute, deliver, or record any deed, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property.

PROPERTY FUNDED INTO A REVOCABLE TRUST REMAINS REACHABLE BY THE SETTLOR'S OWN CREDITORS
So long as Jordan T. Reyes retains the power to revoke The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust, in whole or in part, California law makes the property held in The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust subject to the claims of Jordan T. Reyes's own creditors, to the extent of that power of revocation, throughout Jordan T. Reyes's lifetime. Funding The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust — moving property into Jordan T. Reyes's name as trustee — changes who holds legal title and how the property is administered, but under this statute it does not, by itself, put that property beyond the reach of Jordan T. Reyes's own creditors while The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust remains revocable and Jordan T. Reyes is alive.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the settlor retains the power to revoke the trust in whole or in part, the trust property is subject to the claims of creditors of the settlor to the extent of the power of revocation during the lifetime of the settlor."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 18200 (California Legislative Information text), revocable trust property remains subject to the settlor's creditors during the settlor's lifetime (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=18200.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuinely counter-intuitive consequence of funding a revocable trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust or a specific creditor's claim. This is a single statutory section (§ 18200); no additional independent source was found for this. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself transfer any property into any trust, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property, or whether any specific creditor actually has a claim against it.

A STATUTORY SAFETY VALVE FOR INCOMPLETE FUNDING: THE “HEGGSTAD PETITION”
California law lets a trustee, or any interested person, petition the court for an order under Probate Code Part 19 where the trustee is in possession of or holds title to property claimed to belong to someone else, or where the trustee claims property whose title or possession is held by someone else. This second situation is the one that matters for incomplete funding: where Jordan T. Reyes intended specific property to belong to The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust but title was never formally transferred into Jordan T. Reyes's name as trustee, Jordan T. Reyes or another interested person may petition the probate court to confirm that the property should be treated as belonging to The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust. This procedure is commonly called a “Heggstad petition,” after Estate of Heggstad (1993) 16 Cal.App.4th 943, a published California Court of Appeal decision applying this statute to property a settlor had identified in a signed declaration of trust but never separately deeded to the trustee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(3) The trustee or any interested person in any of the following cases: (A) Where the trustee is in possession of, or holds title to, real or personal property, and the property, or some interest, is claimed to belong to another. (B) Where the trustee has a claim to real or personal property, title to or possession of which is held by another."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 850(a)(3)(A)-(B) (California Legislative Information text), a trustee or interested person may petition the court over property the trustee claims but does not hold title to (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=850.)
  "16 Cal.App.4th 943 (1993) 20 Cal. Rptr.2d 433 Estate of HALVARD L. HEGGSTAD, Deceased. GLEN P. HEGGSTAD, as Trustee, etc., Petitioner and Respondent, v. NANCY RHODES HEGGSTAD, Objector and Appellant. Docket No. A055005. Court of Appeals of California, First District, Division Two. June 21, 1993."
  — Estate of Heggstad (Heggstad v. Heggstad), 16 Cal. App. 4th 943, 20 Cal. Rptr. 2d 433 (Cal. Ct. App., 1st Dist., Div. 2, 1993), Docket No. A055005 (CourtListener case record), case identity and official citation only — confirms this case exists as described, not its holding language (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2253427/heggstad-v-heggstad/)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute and one state's case law, used as real evidence of an actual, sourced safety valve California provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, or that every state provides an equivalent procedure. § 850(a)(3)(A) and (a)(3)(B) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not two independent ones. On Estate of Heggstad specifically: this document verified the case's existence, its correct case name, official citation (16 Cal.App.4th 943, 20 Cal. Rptr.2d 433), court (California Court of Appeal, First District, Division Two), docket number (A055005), and decision date (June 21, 1993) directly against CourtListener's case-law database, fetched independently twice with different request headers and confirmed byte-identical. CourtListener's tool for reading full opinion text was rate-limited during this drafting session (a 125-request daily limit, already exceeded, next available in roughly 12 hours), and a direct fetch of the opinion's own page returned no readable content (HTTP 202 and 403 responses with an empty body) — so the description above of what the court actually held and relied on reflects this case's well-established, widely repeated characterization in later citing authority rather than a quotation independently verified against the primary opinion text in this session; the quoted citation above confirms only the case's identity and official citation, not its substantive holding. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself transfer any property into any trust, file any petition, or determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property or would qualify for this procedure.

PERSONAL PROPERTY: NO DEED REQUIRED, BUT AN UNWRITTEN TRANSFER IS HARD TO PROVE
Unlike real property, personal property carries no general statutory requirement that its transfer into The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust be in writing. But where the only support for treating specific personal property as belonging to The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust is an oral or implied claim — rather than a signed assignment, bill of sale, retitled account, or other written transfer into Jordan T. Reyes's name as trustee — California law holds the claim to a demanding evidentiary standard: the existence and terms of an oral trust of personal property may be established only by clear and convincing evidence, and Jordan T. Reyes's own oral statement that the property belongs to The Jordan T. Reyes Revocable Living Trust, standing alone, is not sufficient evidence that it does.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) The existence and terms of an oral trust of personal property may be established only by clear and convincing evidence. (b) The oral declaration of the settlor, standing alone, is not sufficient evidence of the creation of a trust of personal property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15207(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), an oral trust of personal property requires clear and convincing evidence, and the settlor's own oral statement alone is not enough (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15207.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual evidentiary risk of leaving a personal-property transfer unwritten — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific item of personal property or a specific trust. § 15207(a) and (b) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not two independent ones. This clause does not address the separate title-transfer or registration procedures that apply to specific categories of personal property, such as vehicles, securities, or financial accounts — those are governed by other law outside this document's scope. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself transfer any property into any trust, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property.
